summary: Jesus gives the Twelve authority over demons and disease, sends them two by two through Galilee to preach, and prepares them for both welcome and persecution.
key_insight: Jesus first told His disciples to pray that the Lord of the harvest would send out laborers (Matthew 9:38). In the very next verse He calls the Twelve and sends them. The men who were told to pray for workers became the answer to that prayer.
story: Jesus went through all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom and healing every kind of sickness. When He saw the crowds, He was moved with compassion, because they were weary and scattered, like sheep having no shepherd. He said to His disciples, “The harvest truly is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into His harvest.” {Mt}

Then He called the Twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons, and to cure diseases. {Lk} He began to send them out two by two. {Mk} They were not to go to Gentiles or Samaritans, but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. As they went, they were to preach, “The kingdom of heaven is at hand,” to heal the sick, cleanse lepers, raise the dead and cast out demons. “Freely you have received, freely give.” {Mt}

They were to travel light: no bag, no bread, no money in their belts, and not two tunics. Mark says they were to take a staff and wear sandals. {Mk} Luke lists staffs among the things to leave behind, {Lk} and Matthew lists sandals and staffs, “for a worker is worthy of his food.” {Mt} In each town they were to stay in one house until they left. Where no one would receive them or hear their words, they were to shake the dust off their feet as a testimony against that place.

Then Jesus told them plainly what lay ahead: “Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents and harmless as doves.” They would be handed over to councils, scourged in synagogues, brought before governors and kings, and hated for His name’s sake. The Spirit of their Father would give them words when they were on trial, and “he who endures to the end will be saved.” {Mt}

“Therefore do not fear them,” He said. Not one sparrow falls to the ground apart from the Father’s will, and the very hairs of their heads are numbered. “Therefore whoever confesses Me before men, him I will also confess before My Father who is in heaven.” He had not come to bring peace but a sword, and whoever does not take his cross and follow Him is not worthy of Him. {Mt}

Yet whoever welcomed them would be welcoming Him: “He who receives you receives Me, and he who receives Me receives Him who sent Me.” Even a cup of cold water given to one of these little ones would not lose its reward. {Mt}

So the Twelve went out through the towns and preached that people should repent. They cast out many demons, anointed many sick people with oil, and healed them. {Mk} When Jesus had finished instructing them, He went on to teach and preach in their cities. {Mt}
differences: Mark says Jesus allowed “a staff” and told them to wear sandals; Luke says “neither staffs,” and Matthew says “nor sandals, nor staffs.”
Matthew alone gives the long charge of chapter 10, including the limit to “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” and the warnings of persecution.
Only Mark says they went out two by two and anointed the sick with oil.
Matthew introduces the sending with Jesus’ compassion and the call to pray for laborers; Mark sets it right after the rejection at Nazareth.
The message is “The kingdom of heaven is at hand” in Matthew, “the kingdom of God” in Luke, and “that people should repent” in Mark.

fit.question: Mark says the Twelve could take “a staff” and wear sandals. Matthew says “nor sandals, nor staffs,” and Luke says “neither staffs.” Did Jesus allow a staff or not?

points.label: “Provide” in Matthew
points.text: Matthew’s verb is “Provide” (10:9), which means to get or acquire. Jesus was telling them not to go out and buy gear for the trip. Mark tells them to go with the staff and sandals they already had.

points.label: No spares
points.text: In the NKJV, Matthew and Luke both say “staffs,” plural (some manuscripts read the singular), alongside the ban on “two tunics.” The point is no extra equipment. One staff in hand and the sandals on their feet fit all three accounts.

points.label: One point
points.text: All three agree on what matters: travel light, depend on God, and let those you serve provide your food.

fit.note: The writers report one instruction from different angles, and its purpose is unmistakable in all three.
fit.short: Matthew forbids acquiring new gear; Mark allows the staff and sandals they already had. No spares: travel light and trust God.

scene.label: Two by two
scene.text: The Law required two witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15). Pairs could also help and encourage each other. The pattern continued in the early church: Paul and Barnabas, Peter and John.

scene.label: Traveling gear
scene.text: A traveler carried a staff for walking and protection, a bag for bread and supplies, and coins tied in his belt. A second tunic was a spare layer for cold nights. The Twelve were to leave all the extras and rely on hospitality, which Israel treated as a sacred duty.

scene.label: Shaking off the dust
scene.text: Devout Jews were said to shake off the dust of Gentile lands when they came home. Doing this as they left a Jewish town was a solemn warning that it had shut out God’s message. Paul and Barnabas did it at Antioch in Pisidia (Acts 13:51).

scene.label: Anointing with oil
scene.text: Olive oil was a common remedy for wounds and sickness (Luke 10:34), and anointing was a sign of God’s blessing. The early church kept the practice with prayer (James 5:14).

witnesses.matthew: Turns the sending into the second of five great teaching blocks in his Gospel, each closing with words like “when Jesus finished” (11:1). Matthew’s charge looks past this short trip to the church’s later mission: governors, kings, Gentiles and a gospel that divides families.
witnesses.mark: Keeps it brief and practical: two by two, a staff, sandals, one house, dust shaken off. Then Mark tells John the Baptist’s death while the Twelve are away (6:14–29) before their return (6:30), so the cost of preaching repentance hangs over the mission.
witnesses.luke: Stresses that Jesus gave them “power and authority” and sent them to preach the kingdom of God and heal. Luke will later tell of a second sending, the seventy (10:1), and at the Last Supper Jesus will ask, “did you lack anything?” (22:35).

seeing.reveals: Jesus shares His own authority and His own mission with ordinary men. He sends them as the Father sent Him, so that whoever receives them receives Him and the Father who sent Him.
seeing.living: Jesus told His disciples to pray for workers and then sent the ones who prayed. If you have been praying for someone to reach your neighbors, expect Him to send you. Go lighter than feels safe, trusting the Father who numbers the hairs of your head.
seeing.ponder: What are you holding on to for security that makes it hard to go where Jesus sends you?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus sends the people who pray for the harvest into the harvest.
preaching.watch_for: The prayer of 9:38 is answered in 10:1. Watch also the shift at 10:16–23: Jesus looks beyond this short trip in Galilee to councils, governors and Gentiles, the church’s later mission.
